To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) family caregivers of older adults with chronic illness and dementia are at high risk for physical health and mental health problems, (b) caregiver intervention studies are generally of poor methodological quality, (c) caregiver interventions are effective for reducing caregiver depression and burden and for improving caregiver well-being, but they have little or no effect on caregiver physical health, and (d) there are no data to support the effectiveness of caregiver interventions for improving the health and well-being of persons with dementia

(1) family caregivers are at risk for negative health outcomes, including increased depression, anxiety, and physical health problems; and (2) psychosocial interventions can reduce caregiver burden, distress, depression, and anxiety.

(1) the burden and stress of elder caregiving can be reduced by caregiver support and training interventions; and (2) caregiver interventions are associated with reduced depressive symptoms and reduced rates of institutionalization.
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the role of the family in caring for older persons with chronic illness and disabilities and the impact of caregiving on the physical and mental health and well-being of family caregivers.

the development and evaluation of psychosocial interventions that address the needs of caregivers and their care recipients, and with the development of interventions that target caregivers and care recipients together.
the study of the effects of the social environment on the development and maintenance of mental health.

there is no clear evidence of efficacy of any of the caregiver interventions studied in the past 7 years.
the evidence is not strong enough to support the effectiveness of any of the caregiver intervention programs that have been tested in the RCTs.

the current evidence does not support any specific caregiver intervention as superior to others in reducing the burden, distress and negative health effects of caring for an older relative with disability.

there is a growing body of research that supports the efficacy of caregiver interventions, but the field has yet to identify interventions that are both effective and cost-effective.
